newsitem.title: CHINA: U.S. official vows new progress in China ties.
newsitem.headline: U.S. official vows new progress in China ties.

text.p: U.S. National Security Adviser Sandy Berger pledged on Monday to co-operate with China to make new progress in bilateral ties, the Xinhua news agency said.

"The U.S. side is willing to collaborate with the Chinese in making new progress in the bilateral relationship," Xinhua quoted Berger as telling Liu Huaqiu, director of the Foreign Affairs Office under China's State Council, or cabinet, during talks in Beijing.

The U.S. embassy in Beijing declined to give details of Berger's talks which were expected to focus on plans for China's president and Communist Party chief, Jiang Zemin, to visit the United States in late October for a summit with President Bill Clinton.
Xinhua quoted Liu as saying both sides should have a positive and realistic attitude toward differences between the two countries.
China and the United States have squabbled over a range of issues, including Beijing's rival Taipei, human rights abuses in China and Tibet, trade and nuclear proliferation.
Liu said there were many prospects for bilateral ties as long as both sides conducted dialogue on equal footing, avoided differences and boosted cooperation.
"The two countries... hope to maintain world peace and stability and avoid the chaos of wars and are ready to increase strategic dialogues and cooperation," Xinhua said.
"Preventing the spread of nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction is a common goal of the two countries," the news agency said.

Berger arrived on Sunday and was expected to meet Jiang Zemin on Tuesday in the seaside resort of Beidaihe where China's leaders are gathered to decide policy and personnel changes for the next five years. Berger is due to leave China on Wednesday.

Xinhua said the two countries should work together to prepare Jiang's U.S. trip and ensure its success so that the Sino-U.S. relationship will enter into a new period of development on the eve of the new century.

Jiang's meeting with Clinton will be the first state visit to the United States by a Chinese president since the Chinese army crushed student-led pro-democracy demonstrations in Beijing's Tiananmen Square on June 3-4, 1989.

On Sunday, Jiang stressed the importance of Sino-U.S. ties, saying he wanted to see China and the United States seize on a recent improvement in their rocky relationship as a foundation for healthy long-term contacts.

However, Jiang told visiting U.S. Republican Senator Strom Thurmond, a staunch supporter of Taiwan, that continued improvement in Sino-U.S. ties could only come as long as Washington did not waver in its recognition of Beijing as the sole, legitimate government of all China.
Washington switched diplomatic recognition to Beijing from Taipei in 1979. Beijing considers Taiwan a rebel province and has sought to push the island into diplomatic isolation.

Sino-U.S. ties soured in March 1996 when Washington threw its weight behind Taipei by sending aircraft carriers to waters near Taiwan where China was conducting intimidatory war games in the run-up to the island's first direct presidential elections.
